opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at that time it felt like the most interesting place to be if you cared about intelligence that actually touches the physical world. Around 2016, deep learning was exploding in vision and language, and there was this sense that the same wave would eventually reach robotics. But when I looked at what robots could actually do, there was a huge gap. They were impressive in factories, very precise and very repetitive, but put them in a messy kitchen or ask them to handle something soft or unfamiliar, and they would fall apart.

So part of my motivation was curiosity about that gap. Why is something a toddler does effortlessly, like picking up a cup, so hard for a machine? I felt that to really understand it, I needed to learn the fundamentals first: kinematics, dynamics, control, planning, all the classical machinery that people had built over decades. A traditional robotics group gave me that grounding. You learn to respect the physics, the hardware, the fact that real motors heat up and sensors are noisy and things break.

The other part was a kind of bet. I thought that if learning-based methods were going to transform robotics, the people best positioned to make that happen would be the ones who understood both sides, the classical rigor and the new data-driven tools. Coming purely from machine learning, it's easy to underestimate how hard the real world is. Coming purely from classical robotics, it's easy to dismiss learning as unreliable. I wanted to stand in between.

And to be honest, I also just loved working with real machines. There's something very satisfying, and very humbling, about writing code and then watching a robot either do the right thing or do something completely ridiculous in front of you. That feedback loop kept me hooked.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a very calculated decision at the time. Around 2016 and 2017, deep learning had already blown up in vision and language, and a lot of people my age were rushing toward that. But I kept feeling that the most interesting problem wasn't recognizing an image, it was getting a machine to actually do something in the physical world. Robotics felt like the place where perception, decision-making, and control all had to meet, and where the gap between what worked in a paper and what worked on real hardware was still enormous.

The group I joined was, by today's standards, very traditional. It was about kinematics, dynamics, motion planning, control theory. There was very little learning in it. Some friends thought that was a step backward. But I wanted that foundation. I wanted to understand why a robot arm shakes, why a planner fails in a cluttered scene, why a controller that looks fine in simulation falls apart on a real motor with backlash and latency. You can't appreciate what learning can fix if you've never fought those problems by hand.

There was also a more personal reason. I'd spent a lot of time in front of a screen, and I wanted to build something I could touch. The first time a robot I had programmed picked something up and put it down where it was supposed to go, that feeling was completely different from seeing a loss curve go down. That hooked me.

Looking back, I think the timing was lucky. I got the classical training right before learning-based methods really took over robotics, so I ended up with one foot in each world. A lot of what I do now is basically translating between those two camps.
